Digital advocacy page · MO-ENV076

From our rivers to our seas, what we throw away comes back to us.

Most of the plastic in Philippine waters was never collected on land. Help stop it at the source.

Why it matters

Ocean plastic is a land problem first

Only about 8.8 percent of the country's mismanaged plastic reaches the sea, but that small share is still more than 0.3 million tons a year (World Bank, 2025). Floods carry what the barangay never collected into drains, rivers and Manila Bay.

The fixes already exist. The question is which one gets funded first.

The problem in numbers
0.3M+metric tons a year leak into the sea

World Bank, Dec 2025, as reported by Manila Bulletin, 5 Jan 2026. Limit: I read news coverage of the report.

8.8%of mismanaged plastic reaches the sea

World Bank, Dec 2025. My arithmetic: 0.3M ÷ 0.088 is about 3.4M tons mismanaged a year, a minimum.

164Msachets a day, plus 48M shopping bags and 45M thin-film bags

World Bank via Manila Bulletin. Disputed detail: SunStar and Radar cite DENR at 163M. I follow the World Bank.

900+plastic additives identified in Philippine marine plastic; some found in human and marine samples

Marine Pollution Bulletin, peer-reviewed. Limit: shows exposure is possible, not proven harm.

Causes

Sachets, weak collection, floods

Cheap single-use packaging, under half of plastic reaching sanitary landfills, and rain that washes the rest into rivers (World Bank; Daily Tribune, 2026).

Effects

Ecosystems, livelihoods, floods

Contaminated reefs, animals that eat plastic, fisherfolk who lose income, and clogged waterways that worsen floods.

Where it flows

Rivers carry it to the bay

Cagayan de Oro River: 32nd among the world's plastic-emitting rivers, about 3,600 t a year (PMC study). Manila Bay region: 3,500 to 4,400 t a year projected (The Ocean Cleanup, 2026).

What is already being done

Producer responsibility: EPR Act (RA 11898)

Large companies must recover the packaging they sell. 2025 recovery: 55.98% against a 40% target, across 1,017 companies.

Effective so farLikely to last

DENR via Manila Bulletin, 12 Feb 2026. Limit: self-reported, and recovery is not the same as less plastic in the sea.

Local collection: RA 9003 and barangay MRFs

The 25-year-old law requires segregation and an MRF in every barangay. Last audit: 39% of barangays had one; 29% of LGUs had a sanitary landfill.

PartialNeeds funding

COA data via BAN Toxics and SunStar, 4 Feb 2026. Limit: quoted by an advocacy group; the COA report should be checked.

River barriers: Ocean Cleanup Interceptors

Barriers that catch floating plastic before the bay, starting with the Meycauayan River: 370 to 540 t a year, roughly 8 to 15% of the region's plastic.

Too early to tellTreats the symptom

The Ocean Cleanup press release, 28 Apr 2026. Limit: the group's own statement; no Philippine results yet. Share is my arithmetic.

How I checked

Official data first

World Bank, DENR, COA and peer-reviewed studies first; then national newspapers; then advocacy groups and program releases.

How I checked

Every source has a limit

DENR's EPR results are self-reported. BAN Toxics is an advocate. The Ocean Cleanup describes its own program. Each limit is noted where used.

How I checked

Disputed claims are labelled

Estimates run from about 20,000 t (The Ocean Cleanup) to 0.75 million t (one news report). I follow the World Bank and show the rest.

My advocacy

Stop it at the source, fund the barangay first

Why I made this page, what I concluded, and what I ask you to do.

IHD
Ilog Hanggang DagatWhy I made this page

Because the problem starts at my own sink and sari-sari store

More than 0.3 million tons of plastic leave the Philippines for the sea each year, most of it household waste that was never collected (World Bank, 2025). Ocean plastic felt far away until I traced it back to my own street. The name says it: ilog hanggang dagat, river to sea.

#IlogHanggangDagat #RiverToSea

IHD
Ilog Hanggang DagatWhat I stand for

Facts first, blame last, action always

Evidence: every number has a source. Shared responsibility: households, barangays, companies and agencies each hold a piece of the fix. Prevention: stopping plastic on land beats catching it at sea.

#SourcedNotGuessed

IHD
Ilog Hanggang DagatHow I engage people

Small, checkable steps, shared with sources

I do not ask anyone to save the ocean. I ask for two habits, one visit to the barangay MRF, and one sourced fact shared onward. Plain language, one number at a time. Corrections welcome.

#PickTwoHabits

Conclusions and recommendation

What I concluded from the evidence

Evidence

8.8% of mismanaged plastic reaches the sea, over 0.3M t a year (World Bank, 2025). Floods carry uncollected waste to rivers (Daily Tribune, 2026).

1. Ocean plastic is a collection problem before it is an ocean problem.

Evidence

EPR recovered 55.98% against a 40% target (DENR, 2026); only 39% of barangays had an MRF (COA via SunStar, 2026).

2. Making producers pay works, but it depends on barangay collection that is still missing in most places.

Evidence

One Interceptor: roughly 8 to 15% of the region's projected plastic, 1 to 3% of the national estimate (my calculation; The Ocean Cleanup, 2026).

3. Cleanups are a necessary backstop, not a cure.

Evidence

About 164M sachets a day, roughly 60 billion a year (World Bank; my arithmetic). RA 9003 has asked households to segregate for 25 years.

4. Habits matter at this scale, but only alongside affordable refills and real enforcement.

My recommendation

Fund the barangay first.

Give every barangay a working MRF with regular collection, because producer recovery, flood control and river cleanups all fail without it. Households segregate and choose refills; companies meet and publish EPR targets; agencies publish audited numbers.

Courses of action

What each of us must do

Four levels, because no single level can fix this alone.

Households
  • Segregate biodegradable, recyclable and residual waste.
  • Choose refills over sachets where they exist.
  • Keep canals and storm drains clear.
  • Know which river your street drains into.
Barangay and city
  • Build or fix the MRF and run regular collection.
  • Enforce RA 9003 segregation rules.
  • Close open dumpsites near waterways.
  • Publish collection rates residents can check.
Companies
  • Meet and publish EPR recovery targets.
  • Sell refill and bulk formats at sachet prices.
  • Redesign packaging so it can be recycled locally.
National agencies
  • Audit EPR results independently.
  • Fund MRFs in the 61% of barangays without one.
  • Pair river Interceptors with upstream collection.

Shared posts and media

News reports and campaign posts from others, each shared with a caption of my own. Every item is credited to its source.

IHD
Ilog Hanggang DagatShared post · caption by the author

Kailangan bang umabot sa ganito?

Caption: WWF-Philippines asked this in 2018, warning of "more plastic than fish." Eight years on, the numbers have not turned: about 164 million sachets a day and over 0.3 million tons reaching the sea each year (World Bank, 2025). The ask is unchanged: refuse the plastic you can, and make your barangay collect the rest.

#AyokoNgPlastik #IlogHanggangDagat

IHD
Ilog Hanggang DagatShared video · caption by the author

Why the sachet is not the villain, and not innocent either

Caption: A sachet is the only size many families can afford that day, so "stop buying sachets" is not a plan. Yet 164 million are used daily and most cannot be recycled. That is why the recommendation here targets companies (refills at sachet prices under EPR) and barangays (collect what is left), not the buyer.

#IlogHanggangDagat

Shared article · Manila Bulletin, 12 Feb 2026EPR law proves its impact as plastic recovery rates surge nationwide

Caption: Companies recovered almost 56% of covered plastic once the law made them pay for it. The next question: where does it go after recovery?

Shared article · SunStar Davao, 4 Feb 2026BAN Toxics: Invest in effective solid waste law implementation
